sections.h2: Where does a Madison County deed get recorded?
sections.html:
In London, at the courthouse. The Madison County Recorder sits at 1 N Main St, Room 40, London, OH 43140, and takes calls at 740-852-1854. The counter opens at 8 AM and closes at 4 PM on weekdays, though recording ends at 3:30 PM, so a deed handed over at 3:45 waits until the next business day.

Electronic recording is available through four named platforms: CSC eRecording (866-652-0111), Simplifile, ePN and Hopdox. Ask your title company or attorney which platform they use, since the deed can then be recorded without a trip to the courthouse.

sections.h2: What is the recording fee in Madison County?
sections.html:
A two-page deed is $39.00 and each extra page is $8.00, a schedule in effect since January 1, 2025 per the Recorder. Senate Bill 94 added a $5.00 surcharge to most documents, the page explains, to fund the preservation and digitizing of records and the office's running costs, and it points to section 317.32.

That statute shows how the amount is built: half base fee, half housing trust fund fee, plus an optional county surcharge. Copies, certified copies, references to older documents and zoning filings carry their own listed amounts. Phone 740-852-1854 to price any unusual document before you mail payment.

sections.h2: How far back do Madison County's online land records reach?
sections.html:
Different record types start at different dates, according to the Recorder's own note. Checking the right category saves a trip to the courthouse:

Online coverage listed on the Madison County Recorder's page
Record typeCoverage stated
DeedsScanned, indexed and online from March 1, 1920 to present
Mortgages, indexingIndexed from July 17, 1964
Mortgages, imagesScanned and indexed from September 25, 1968
Miscellaneous, lease, lien, federal tax lien, mechanics lien, unemployment compensation lien, mortgage releaseHistorical Archive online, dating to at least 1980, some older

All the original books remain in the office. If a search turns up a gap, call the counter and ask staff to follow up in the books.

sections.h2: What does the Madison County Auditor do with a deed first?
sections.html:
Ohio makes the Auditor endorse the deed before the Recorder files it. Under section 319.202, the buyer's representative submits a statement of value, or a statement of the exemption reason, and the Auditor notes the conveyance fee on the deed itself.

The Madison County Auditor is at 1 N Main St, PO Box 47, London, OH 43140-0047, phone 740-852-9717, weekdays 8 AM to 4 PM. Its property transfer forms page lists the packet pieces a closer may need:

  • DTE 100, the conveyance fee statement of value and receipt.
  • DTE 100EX, the statement of the reason for an exemption.
  • DTE 101, a statement of conveyance of homestead property.
  • DTE 102, a statement of conveyance of current agricultural use valuation property.
  • DTE 100M and DTE 41 for manufactured or mobile homes.
  • Affidavits of trustee and successor trustee under sections 317.22 and 5302.171.

The Auditor's site also carries a conveyance fee calculator under its Tools menu. Run your sale through it, or phone the office, rather than guessing at the county's rate.

sections.h2: How does the Auditor treat sale price and gifts?
sections.html:
For an arm's length sale, the Auditor's measure under section 319.202 is everything paid or promised, including any mortgage balance the buyer takes over. For a gift, the measure shifts to what the house would sell for on the open market. Misstating either figure on purpose is unlawful.

The buyer's statement also answers two questions. Was the seller asked whether tax reductions for owner occupancy or homestead apply? Was the land under the agricultural use valuation? A yes to either needs a sworn instrument attached. If the house is a rental, the endorsement points the buyer to a landlord filing under section 5323.02.

sections.h2: Which rules govern conveyance fee amounts in Madison County?
sections.html:
Two statutes work together. Section 319.54(G)(3) sets the state charge at a dollar or a dime per hundred, whichever is bigger. Section 322.02 lets commissioners layer on a local tax up to thirty cents per hundred, owed by the grantor.

Exemptions cover several family and estate situations:

  • Gifts within a marriage, or handed down to a son or daughter.
  • Transfers among the heirs of one decedent when nobody pays money.
  • Moves into or out of a revocable trust.
  • A corrective deed that fixes an earlier recorded deed.

The exemption reason belongs on the form.

sections.h2: What is Madison County like around London?
sections.html:
Madison County lies in central Ohio west of Franklin County, with London as the seat and largest city. Wikipedia gives the area as 467 square miles with almost no water, and places the county in the Columbus metro area. Interstates 70 and 71 cross it on the way to Columbus, and a sliver of Dublin lies inside the county line.

QuickFacts puts Madison County at 46,985 residents in mid-2025, up 7.1 percent since the 2020 base, with 17,383 housing units. Over 2020 to 2024, a typical owned home was valued at $250,100 and a typical household earned $87,045. Owners occupy 77.5 percent of homes, rent runs a median $943, and the mean commute runs 24.9 minutes. The Auditor has also finished a countywide reappraisal for tax year 2026, with tentative values shown for each parcel on its website, so sellers should look up their own parcel before setting a price.

sections.h2: Who else works in Madison County, and what borders it?
sections.html:
London is the seat and the largest city. Madison County was established in 1810 and named for James Madison. In 1850 it counted 10,015 residents, mostly in farming, and in 2020 it counted 43,824. Wikipedia also lists the Ohio Peace Officer Training Academy and the state Bureau of Criminal Identification and Investigation among its institutions.

Neighbors include Union and Champaign counties to the north and northwest, Franklin County to the east, Pickaway to the southeast, Fayette to the south, and Greene and Clark to the west. An owner with land across a county line needs a separate recorder and auditor filing in each county.

faqs.q: When does Madison County stop recording each day?
faqs.a: 3:30 PM. The office is open until 4 PM on weekdays but stops recording at 3:30, so deliver deeds earlier in the afternoon or use an e-recording service.

faqs.q: What is Madison County's price for recording a deed?
faqs.a: A two-page deed is $39.00 and each extra page is $8.00, a schedule in effect since January 1, 2025 per the Recorder. Check with the office for extra charges that apply to references, copies or special filings.

faqs.q: Can I e-record a deed in Madison County?
faqs.a: Yes. The Recorder names CSC eRecording, Simplifile, ePN and Hopdox as the electronic routes. Ask your title company or attorney which one they use.

faqs.q: Does the Madison County Auditor have a form for a trust or estate transfer?
faqs.a: Its forms page lists DTE 100EX for exemption reasons and affidavits for a trustee or successor trustee under Revised Code sections 317.22 and 5302.171. An attorney should pick the right ones for your situation.

faqs.q: How old are Madison County's scanned deeds?
faqs.a: Deeds are scanned, indexed and online from March 1, 1920 forward, according to the Recorder. Mortgages are scanned and indexed from September 25, 1968, and the original books stay in the office.
